4.en: ‘And yet you accuse me of being a madman, you who have never had your sanity tested so sorely. What right have you to call me heretic and blasphemer, who have not heard the whisper of the dark gods in your ear? You are weak. Vulnerable. Human in your frailty. I am strong, and yet you still judge me for my sins, thou who art most sinful to the heart? Every scholam child knows, “Only the insane have strength enough to prosper: only those who prosper truly judge what is sane”.’

28.en: Each Inquisitor interprets Imperial doctrine differently. Given time and exposure to the Imperium’s greatest threats and the terrifying consequences of failure, their beliefs and ideals are tested constantly. Inquisitors find new ways to tread the line between faith and heresy to survive and succeed at their mission. However, new ways of thinking can harden into steadfast ideals that separate them further from the Imperial creed and their peers.

48.en: Most began their great mission as Puritans, their ascension to ultimate authority founded on their Holy Order’s or predecessor’s traditionalist beliefs. It is not until their beliefs are thoroughly tested that most Inquisitors begin to deviate towards Radicalism — when presented with a problem that requires drastic measures to solve. Some Inquisitors are well aware of the schisms their newfound actions and beliefs cause and the price it puts upon their head, so they often hide their true Philosophy behind one more traditionally accepted by their peers.

52.en: All these Philosophies, Puritan or Radical, have rich names and mystic ideals. But to an acolyte, initially, these points mean little. Rarely will an acolyte know of the particulars of their Inquisitor’s Philosophy; they are expected to believe in their Inquisitor no matter what they observe or are ordered to do.
